title: Volusia & Flagler Real Estate Operations Reference
metaDesc: Which Realtor association and MLS each Volusia and Flagler city falls under, and the local sign rules, in one reference. Four associations, two MLS systems.
h1: The Volusia & Flagler Real Estate Operations Reference
about: A consolidated operational reference for real estate agents working in Volusia and Flagler County, Florida: Realtor association and MLS membership by city, and residential for-sale sign regulations by jurisdiction.

hub.name: Become a Real Estate Agent in Florida

answer: Four separate Realtor associations cover Volusia and Flagler County, running on two different MLS systems, and which one applies to you follows your office location rather than your home address. The Daytona Beach Area association covers the northeast coast on its own MLS; West Volusia covers the inland St. Johns corridor, New Smyrna Beach Board covers the southeast, and Flagler County covers Palm Coast, Flagler Beach and Bunnell, all three on Stellar MLS. Sign rules are set city by city: unincorporated Volusia allows 4.5 square feet set back 5 feet for three months a year, while Palm Coast allows two signs at 6 square feet each and requires removal within three days of closing.
takeaways: Four associations and two MLS systems cover two counties. Most Florida counties have one of each, so advice written for the rest of the state is wrong here.
The Daytona Beach Area association runs its own MLS. The other three are on Stellar MLS. This is the detail that most often catches out an agent moving in.
Your association follows the office your license is registered to, not where you live.
Sign rules change at every city line. Unincorporated Volusia allows 4.5 square feet; Palm Coast allows 6 and starts a three-day removal clock at closing.
Florida law protects a security-company sign near your door. It does not protect a for-sale sign, so HOA covenants can be stricter than the city code.
tldr: One reference for the operational facts that are specific to this market: association and MLS by city for all nineteen cities, the four association profiles, and residential sign rules by jurisdiction. The market is fragmented in a way national guidance consistently gets wrong, and the figures here come from the association charters and municipal codes rather than from summaries of them.
body:
What this page is

This is the operational reference for working as a real estate agent in Volusia and Flagler County: which Realtor association and multiple listing service you end up in, and what the local sign rules actually say. It exists because this market is unusually fragmented and no national source gets it right. Most Florida counties map one county to one association and one MLS. This two-county market has four associations and two different MLS systems, and the boundaries do not follow the county line.

Every figure below is drawn from the association charters and the municipal codes themselves. Where something has not been verified, the table says so rather than guessing, because a wrong setback figure is worse than no setback figure.

Membership follows the location of the office your license is registered to, not your home address. An agent living in DeLand but working from a Daytona Beach office joins the Daytona Beach Area association, not West Volusia.

The four associations, and the one that works differently

Table 2 — The four associations
AssociationServing sinceCoverageMLS
Daytona Beach Area Association of Realtors1922Northeast coastal VolusiaIts own MLS, separate from the other three
New Smyrna Beach Board of Realtors1945Southeast VolusiaStellar MLS, shareholder since September 2023
West Volusia Association of Realtors1963Inland Volusia, St. Johns River corridorStellar MLS
Flagler County Association of Realtors—All of Flagler CountyStellar MLS, shareholder since 2022

Stellar MLS is the current name for what was My Florida Regional MLS until its 2019 rebrand. Three of the four associations here run on it. The Daytona Beach Area association is the outlier and runs its own system, which is the single detail that most often surprises an agent moving into this market.

Where you can legally put a sign

Sign placement looks like common sense until you read the code and discover it is a patchwork. The two jurisdictions below differ on maximum size, on setback, on how many signs are allowed, on whether an open-house sign is separately permitted, and on how long the sign may stay up. An agent who assumes the rule they learned in one city travels to the next one will be wrong somewhere in this market.

Table 3 — Residential for-sale sign rules, by jurisdiction
JurisdictionMax sizeSetbackHow many, and how long
Unincorporated Volusia County4.5 sq ft5 ftOne per 1,000 ft of street frontage, up to three months a year
Palm Coast6 sq ft2 ft front, 15 ft sideTwo visible from adjacent rights-of-way, down within three days of closing
Other incorporated citiesNot yet verified against the municipal code. Volusia contains sixteen incorporated cities and Flagler several more, each writing its own sign code. Read the code for the city you are listing in, or ask us.

Unincorporated Volusia’s 4.5 square feet applies in the R-1 to R-6 and R-9 residential classifications; other zoning classifications rise to 32 square feet, which is why a highway commercial listing can carry a far larger sign than a house two streets away. Palm Coast permits one additional open-house sign of up to 9 square feet, and caps sign height at 6 feet.

Three rules that hold everywhere here

Stay out of the public right-of-way. That strip along a road belongs to the government, not the homeowner, and it usually extends several feet past the pavement and often past the sidewalk, including grass a homeowner mows and assumes is theirs. Volusia County’s code prohibits signs on public property or rights-of-way and states that a sign erected in violation may be removed.

Do not attach a sign to anything vertical that is not yours. Volusia prohibits signs affixed to trees, shrubbery, vines, utility poles or beach dune walkover structures. Palm Coast prohibits attachment to utility poles, trees and traffic control devices, and separately restricts signs mounted to fences. The utility pole rule is not bureaucratic: staples and nails left in a pole are a real hazard to a line worker putting a hand where your sign used to be.

The HOA layer can be stricter, and in Florida it is allowed to be. Some states protect a homeowner’s right to advertise their own property for sale. Florida does not. Under F.S. 720.304(6) a parcel owner may display a reasonably sized sign provided by a contractor for security services within 10 feet of an entrance to the home. That is the whole protection, and there is no companion provision covering a for-sale sign. Inside a deed-restricted community, the recorded covenants set the real limit.

What joining actually costs

There is no single number, and anyone quoting you one is guessing. Expect several layers rather than a flat fee: an application or entrance fee, local association dues, Florida Realtors state dues, National Association of Realtors dues, and a separate MLS access fee on top. Each is structured differently by association and each changes over time.

We deliberately do not publish figures here. A dues number that is a year stale is worse than no number, because someone will budget against it. Confirm current amounts with the specific association your office falls under, and ask your brokerage in writing what it covers or reimburses before you join.

How current this is, and what is not covered

Association names, coverage areas and MLS affiliations reflect the position at the time of writing and are believed accurate. Associations occasionally merge, rebrand or change MLS partners, so confirm current status directly with the association. The sign table covers two jurisdictions in full and explicitly marks the rest as unverified; it is a starting point for the cities it names and a warning for the ones it does not.

The longer explanations behind each of these sit on their own pages: which MLS and Realtor association you join here, where you can legally put a sign, and how you get an MLS lockbox key. If you are weighing which office to work from, what happens to your MLS access when you switch brokerages covers the transfer side.

Once you know which association you are in, the next practical question is what it charges when a rule is broken: what gets you fined by the Daytona Beach MLS.

A second reference worth holding alongside this one covers the condominium rules that now drive fees and assessments: milestone inspections and reserve studies.

faq.q: Which Realtor association do I join in Volusia County?
faq.a: It depends on where your office sits, and Volusia is served by three separate associations. The Daytona Beach Area Association of Realtors covers the northeast coastal corridor: Daytona Beach, Ormond Beach, Port Orange, Ponce Inlet, Daytona Beach Shores, Holly Hill and South Daytona. The West Volusia Association of Realtors covers the inland St. Johns River side: DeLand, Deltona, DeBary, Orange City, Lake Helen and Pierson. The New Smyrna Beach Board of Realtors covers the southeast corner: New Smyrna Beach, Edgewater and Oak Hill. Flagler County has its own association again, covering Palm Coast, Flagler Beach and Bunnell.

faq.q: Is all of Volusia and Flagler County on Stellar MLS?
faq.a: No, and this is the single detail that most often surprises an agent moving into the area. Three of the four local associations are Stellar MLS shareholders: West Volusia, New Smyrna Beach Board, which joined in September 2023, and Flagler County, which joined in 2022. The Daytona Beach Area Association of Realtors is the outlier and runs its own separate MLS system. Stellar MLS is the current name for what was called My Florida Regional MLS until it rebranded in 2019.

faq.q: How big can a for-sale sign be in Volusia County?
faq.a: In unincorporated Volusia County a temporary sign in the R-1 through R-6 and R-9 residential classifications is limited to 4.5 square feet of copy area, roughly an 18 by 36 inch panel, set back 5 feet, one per 1,000 feet of street frontage, and displayed no more than three months a year. Other zoning classifications rise to 32 square feet. Incorporated cities write their own codes, so those figures do not travel: Palm Coast, for example, allows two signs at 6 square feet per street frontage with a 2 foot setback, and requires removal within three days of closing.

faq.q: Can a homeowners association ban a for-sale sign in Florida?
faq.a: Effectively yes, inside a deed-restricted community. Some states protect a homeowner's right to advertise their own property for sale, and Florida is not one of them. The Homeowners' Association Act addresses signs in one narrow place: F.S. 720.304(6) permits a parcel owner to display a reasonably sized sign provided by a contractor for security services within 10 feet of an entrance to the home. There is no companion provision protecting a for-sale sign, so where an association's recorded covenants restrict one, the covenants govern.

faq.q: What does joining a Realtor association and MLS cost here?
faq.a: There is no single figure, and any source quoting you one is guessing. The cost comes in layers: an application or entrance fee, local association dues, Florida Realtors state dues, National Association of Realtors dues, and a separate MLS access fee. Each is structured differently by association and each changes over time, so confirm current amounts with the specific association your office falls under, and ask your brokerage in writing what it covers or reimburses.
